title: America rejects what it seeks to export: The PAX Silica question

blocks.text: The strongest argument against PAX Silica does not come from the Philippines. It comes from the United States itself.
The same country promoting PAX Silica as a secure, clean and modern future for the Philippines is facing resistance to that same future at home.

According to INQUIRER.net, protests against the expansion of AI data centers have taken place in 46 U.S. states, including Texas, Washington, Utah, Virginia and California, with objections focused on water consumption and effects on electrical grids.

A wider study by GatherGov, which monitored nearly 99,000 local government records in the 12 months ending in September 2026, found that about 2,100 jurisdictions in all 50 states used at least one tool to restrict data center development.
In other words, there is no state in America where the AI buildout is unopposed.

That raises a question for Filipinos: If Americans themselves will not accept AI data centers, advanced manufacturing parks and semiconductor hubs in their communities without strict safeguards, why should Filipinos accept them in Capas, Tarlac, and across 9 million hectares of Philippine land with fewer safeguards?
The ballot revolt of Nov. 3, 2026: 10 states, 40 votes, one verdict
The clearest evidence came in the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, 2026.

In local votes across 10 states — California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, Nevada, New Jersey, North Dakota, Ohio and Wisconsin — residents rejected data centers in 40 of 41 ballot measures, according to Ballotpedia.
Ohio alone had 21 measures, more than any other state, followed by Illinois with seven, Maine with four and Kansas with three.
Voters approved bans, moratoriums, zoning changes and requirements for public votes on large projects. Only one measure, in Harwood, North Dakota, went the industry’s way.
Counting six earlier votes in 2026, the final tally was 46 of 47 decided that year in favor of limits.

In Kansas, voters in El Dorado approved a 10-year ban on high-impact data centers by 71% to 29%, defining high-impact facilities as those using more than 10 megawatts of peak electricity or more than 100,000 gallons of water per day.

In Ohio, voters in Granville, Hubbard and Urbana banned data centers outright, while Conneaut, Defiance and Sunbury capped them at 25 megawatts. Grove City required a public referendum for any large industrial project.
In Maine, towns passed retroactive moratoriums. In Florida, Edgewater amended its charter to bar new data centers from being approved, built, expanded or operated.

An August 2026 Embold Research poll of 2,045 registered voters found that 75% opposed a new data center near their homes. A University of Massachusetts Amherst poll found that only 11% would welcome one.
The issue crossed partisan lines. In a CNBC voter poll, 56% of voters said data centers were a crucial or major factor in their vote.
The governors’ revolt: Nine states holding 41% of U.S. capacity
The resistance did not stop at the local level. It reached governors’ offices.
Of 34 winning candidates for governor in the 2026 elections, 32 support stronger regulation or restrictions, while 12 back bans or moratoriums.
Nine states in which governors or governors-elect have backed or imposed construction pauses now account for 158.6 gigawatts of planned capacity, or 41% of the U.S. development pipeline.
Texas accounts for 88.4 gigawatts, Ohio for 21.9 gigawatts, Georgia for 20.2 gigawatts, New Mexico for 11 gigawatts and New York for 9.9 gigawatts.

In Texas, the state with the most planned AI capacity, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Gov. Greg Abbott after promising a moratorium on new data center construction, stricter rules on water and power use, and an end to tax breaks.
Abbott had already frozen data center grid connections and air permits in August 2026, demanding an audit of power supply, water use and tax incentives through the end of the year.
In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governorship after calling for a pause on new data centers.
In Ohio, Amy Acton beat Vivek Ramaswamy after calling for a conditional moratorium requiring new projects to bear all electricity costs and be built only on former industrial land.
In New Mexico, Deb Haaland pledged a statewide moratorium and won. In Michigan, the incoming governor campaigned on stopping or pausing data center development.
In New York, Gov. Kathy Hochul had already enacted a one-year moratorium on new data centers larger than 50 megawatts. In Oregon, the governor ran on extending the pause already in force.

In Iowa and Nevada, incoming governors want to end tax breaks for AI data centers. In Florida, the next governor promised to require data centers to produce their own electricity instead of drawing from the grid.
Even in Virginia, the data center capital of the world, Gov. Abigail Spanberger campaigned on affordability and making data centers pay their own way.

The state’s Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission found that the industry’s sales tax exemption saved data centers $2.73 billion between 2021 and 2024, representing 53% of everything Virginia spent on business incentives. The exemption amounted to $1.02 billion in 2024 alone.
Why Americans do not want them: Water, power bills, noise, few jobs and loss of public control
The concerns raised by Americans are also relevant to the Philippines, where the same issues of water, power, health, employment and public participation are at stake.
First, water.

In Arizona, Tucson’s City Council voted 7-0 in August 2025 to stop Project Blue, an Amazon-linked data center, after weeks of public pressure. Chandler’s council unanimously rejected a 400,000-square-foot project that sought to use more than 100 million gallons of water a year.

A Ceres report found that data centers in the seven states with the highest concentrations — Virginia, Texas, California, Illinois, Georgia, Ohio and Arizona — use about 3.4 trillion gallons of freshwater for electric power generation every year. That is more than the 8 million acre-feet of average annual urban water demand in California.

In the Philippines, PAX Silica is projected to need 130 million liters of water per day, or 39 billion liters per year, equivalent to the consumption of 600,000 households, in Central Luzon, the country’s rice bowl, where farmers already experience El Niño droughts.
Second, power bills.

In Virginia, residential electricity rates rose 11.3% in August 2026, while rates in Ohio rose 10.4%, compared with a national average increase of 3.4%. Data centers were first in line for power while households paid for transmission upgrades.
Dominion Energy in Virginia reports requests for more than 70 gigawatts of power from data centers, requiring about 233 new substations costing $6 billion to $12 billion.

In the Philippines, PAX Silica will need 3 gigawatts, equivalent to 16% to 20% of Luzon’s peak load, and 3 to 5 gigawatts under some scenarios. The project could raise costs for ordinary Filipinos and reduce available power for households and small industries.
Third, noise and health.

Residents in Loudoun and Prince William counties in Virginia have complained about the continuous low-frequency hum from cooling chillers, diesel backup generators and construction traffic near homes and schools.

In the Philippines, waste heat from AI data centers is projected to raise field temperatures by 4.5 to 6 degrees Celsius, reaching 45 to 47 C at peak. The projected temperatures could cause rice spikelet sterility above 35 to 36 C and make farming nonviable within 12 to 15 kilometers.
Fourth, few jobs and large tax incentives.
In Georgia, the state gave up $474 million in tax breaks in fiscal 2025 and received 1,641 permanent operations jobs, compared with 8,505 construction jobs.
In Virginia, the industry reported $49 billion in investment but only 1,610 net new jobs, equivalent to about $30 million in investment per job.
In Texas, the expected cost of the data center tax break was $180 million over two years, but the comptroller now puts the cost at more than $1 billion in a single year.
In the Philippines, the government promises 130,000 to 200,000 jobs and P180 billion in revenues, but the cost of land, water, power, subsidies and debt has not been independently audited.
Fifth, public participation.
Americans voted after projects were approved with tax breaks, grid connections and water permits before residents were consulted.
Similar concerns have been raised in the Philippines, where no draft of the PAX Silica Framework, feasibility study or Environmental Impact Assessment has been shown to the public.
Why PAX Silica violates Philippine laws: The legal foundation for stopping it
The American resistance is political. The Philippine case is also legal.
As PAX Silica is being pursued, it raises potential violations of the 1987 Constitution and Philippine statutes in at least five areas that could provide a legal basis for stopping its signing.
First, Presidential Decree No. 1586, or the Philippine Environmental Impact Statement System.

There is no feasibility study from which an Environmental Impact Assessment and an Environmental Compliance Certificate can be based. As of August 2026, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources had reported that no EIA for PAX Silica had been applied for or processed.
A project without an EIA and an ECC cannot legally proceed.
Second, Republic Act No. 8371, or the Indigenous Peoples’ Rights Act, and Article XII, Section 5 of the Constitution.

The Bases Conversion and Development Authority claims the 1,620-hectare site as its land, while the site is within the Indigenous Peoples Ancestral Domain Claim Zone of the Aeta Hanguey community in Capas, Tarlac.
No project can proceed in ancestral domains without free, prior and informed consent, or FPIC, obtained under customary law after full disclosure.
Third, Article II, Section 16 of the Constitution, which protects the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology.
The Supreme Court recognized this in Oposa v. Factoran as a fundamental right of present and future generations.

PAX Silica threatens that right through water depletion, wastewater containing chemicals and heavy metals, air pollution from backup generators, deforestation from mining, and heat that could damage rice production.

Fourth, Article XII, Section 2 of the Constitution, which requires that the exploration, development and utilization of natural resources remain under the full control and supervision of the state for the benefit of Filipinos.

Executive Order No. 122, signed Aug. 18, 2026, opens 9 million hectares — 30%, or nearly one-third, of the Philippines’ 30 million hectares — to critical mineral mining exploration and fast-tracked permitting. That represents a roughly 1,000% increase over the current 813,575 hectares of approved mining areas.
The expansion raises questions about whether state control over natural resources would be preserved if the minerals are developed for foreign AI, semiconductor and military production.

Fifth, Article VII, Section 21 of the Constitution and the principle requiring Senate concurrence for treaties.
PAX Silica involves long-term commitments involving land, water, energy, fiscal resources and mineral access that affect national patrimony.

It cannot proceed as a mere executive agreement, note verbale or BCDA deal if those commitments require Senate concurrence. At minimum, the project requires Senate oversight, public consultation and a full, independent cost-benefit analysis.
The U.S. Embassy’s own fact sheet described the zone as combining American expertise, institutions and legal regimes with Philippine workers, minerals and energy.
The U.S. demand for diplomatic immunity and 99-year leases, which would conflict with the constitutional limit of 75 years, further raises questions involving Philippine sovereignty.
Recommendations for the Philippines: Stop the signing
Stopping PAX Silica is possible. Americans imposed restrictions in 40 of 41 votes by using local democratic processes. Filipinos can likewise use existing Philippine laws and institutions.
First, demand no signing without the documents.

The Filipino people, Congress and the Senate should demand that no PAX Silica Framework, lease or memorandum be signed until the full text, feasibility study, Environmental Impact Assessment, water and energy balance, fiscal cost, and subsidy and debt exposure are published in full in Filipino and English.
The documents should also be subjected to 90 days of public consultation in Tarlac, Pampanga, Nueva Ecija and Mindanao.
No document, no signature.
Second, file and support legal actions.

Citizens, Aeta communities, farmers and fisherfolk can file petitions for a writ of kalikasan and writ of continuing mandamus in the Supreme Court, based on the right to a balanced and healthful ecology.
Such petitions could seek to compel the government to conduct a full EIA, respect FPIC and stop any construction, clearing or mining under Executive Order No. 122 until compliance is demonstrated.
Congress can also file a petition questioning Executive Order No. 122 as an unconstitutional delegation of the state’s control over natural resources.
Third, use Congress as a safeguard.
The Senate should pass a resolution requiring Senate concurrence before any PAX Silica agreement takes effect.

The House should act on House Resolution No. 1128, filed by Rep. Renee Co, calling for a full investigation, and block any budget, tax incentive or franchise for PAX Silica in the 2027 General Appropriations Act until the EIA, FPIC and cost-benefit analysis are complete.
The Senate inquiries by Sens. Pangilinan, Imee Marcos and Hontiveros should lead to a joint Senate report with a recommendation on whether to suspend the project.
Fourth, protect the Aetas and farmers first.
The National Commission on Indigenous Peoples should certify whether FPIC has been obtained from the Aeta Hanguey community. If it has not, the commission should issue a cease-and-desist order.

The Department of Agrarian Reform should certify how much agricultural land would be converted, while the Department of Agriculture should certify the project’s impact on rice production in Central Luzon.
No certification, no conversion.
Fifth, build a broad, nonpartisan and evidence-based movement similar to the American movement.
The American opposition included farmers, homeowners, teachers, doctors, Republicans and Democrats who focused on power bills, water and noise rather than ideology.

In the Philippines, such a movement should include Aeta elders, farmers, fisherfolk, teachers, doctors, scientists, lawyers, church leaders and local government officials in Capas, Bamban, Gerona, Victoria, La Paz and Angeles City.

It should demand that data centers and advanced manufacturing facilities pay the full cost of power, water and transmission; be prohibited from using potable water for cooling; use closed-loop cooling systems; be barred from agricultural and ancestral land; and be subject to a moratorium until the scientific assessments are complete.
Sixth, propose a Filipino alternative.
The Philippines does not need to reject technology. It can instead establish safeguards to ensure that development protects Philippine resources and interests.

The proposed alternative is Protect PH First: No PAX Silica signing until the Philippines has a national critical minerals law, a national AI and data center law with water, energy and land caps, a national land use law, and legislation requiring local processing, local value-added activity and Filipino ownership of minerals rather than extraction primarily for foreign AI and military production.
Malaysia and Indonesia have pursued forms of resource nationalism by restricting nickel exports and requiring local processing. The Philippines can pursue a similar policy.
If the United States seeks a genuine partnership, it should operate under Philippine laws, Philippine courts, Philippine taxes and Philippine environmental standards.
Conclusion
If America will not accept it, why should we?

The United States has shown, through resistance in 46 states, 40 of 41 ballot votes and nine states accounting for 41% of its planned AI capacity, that AI data centers, advanced manufacturing parks and semiconductor hubs without adequate safeguards can impose substantial costs on water, electricity, health and public participation.

The Philippines has additional reasons for caution because it has more limited water, power and land resources, as well as constitutional guarantees protecting the right to a balanced and healthful ecology, ancestral domains and state control over natural resources.
BCDA President Bingcang says PAX Silica will operate under Philippine laws.
The project, however, has no feasibility study, EIA, ECC, FPIC or Senate concurrence, while an executive order opens nearly one-third of the country to critical mineral exploration.
The Filipino people have legal protections, scientific concerns and the American experience to consider before the project proceeds.

The signing should be stopped until the documents are made public, the scientific evidence is considered, the Aetas and farmers have given informed consent, and the Senate and the public have had the opportunity to decide.
If the United States will not accept such projects in its own communities without safeguards, the Philippines should not be expected to do so either. /dm
[Dr. Teodoro C. Mendoza, Ph.D. is a former professor of crop science and sustainable agriculture at the University of the Philippines Los Baños.]
